query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing vanadium as an alloying additive into the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy will enable the in situ formation of a stable, lubricious vanadium-rich oxide tribolayer that maintains low friction and reduced wear from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: Standard CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with its typical microstructure and tribological behavior at ambient temperatures.
generation.intervention: Alloying the CoCrFeNi matrix with vanadium at a concentration analogous to that used in related HEA systems (e.g., similar to Al0.7CoCrFeNiV0.5) to promote microstructural homogeneity and oxidic phase formation.
generation.conditions: Sliding tribological tests conducted in ambient air across a temperature range from ~25 °C to 800 °C under high contact pressures (e.g., near 0.936 GPa) and similar loads as used in prior studies.
generation.structural_mediator: A modified microstructure featuring a homogeneous solid solution and, under sliding conditions, a self-forming vanadium-rich oxide layer at the surface.
generation.mechanism: The vanadium additive refines the microstructure and, when exposed to the elevated temperatures during sliding, oxidizes to form a lubricious and protective oxide layer. This tribolayer reduces direct metal–metal contact and shear stress, thereby lowering friction and wear across the entire temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped CoCrFeNi baseline, the vanadium-doped version will exhibit a significantly lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate throughout the temperature range, maintaining performance consistency from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.baseline: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy without any vanadium addition.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective under sliding conditions in ambient air with contact pressures up to ~0.936 GPa and temperatures ranging from approximately 25 °C to 800 °C; performance outside these conditions is not addressed.
generation.uncertainty: The precise oxidation behavior of vanadium at high temperatures in the CoCrFeNi system and the stability/durability of the resulting oxide tribolayer under long-term or cyclic conditions remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one of the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy and one where the alloy is doped with vanadium (at a concentration analogous to that proven effective in related systems). Conduct ball-on-disk sliding tests under identical ambient conditions while progressively increasing the test temperature from room temperature to 800 °C. At predetermined temperature intervals, measure the coefficient of friction and wear rate. Execute post-test surface characterization (using microscopy and oxide phase analysis) to confirm the formation of the vanadium-rich oxide layer in the doped sample.
measurements: Coefficient of friction at fixed temperature increments
Oxide composition analysis (using XPS or EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the vanadium-doped CoCrFeNi alloy does not show a statistically significant reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate across the entire temperature range relative to the baseline, or if no stable vanadium-rich oxide tribolayer is observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
High-entropy alloys are of interest to many researchers due to the possibility of shaping their functional properties by, among other things, the use of alloying additives. One approach to improving the wear resistance of the AlCoCrFeNi alloy is modification through the addition of titanium. However, in this study, an alternative solution was explored by adding vanadium, which has a completely different effect on the material’s structure compared to titanium. The effect of vanadium additives on changes in the microstructure, hardness, and wear resistance of the Al0.7CoCrFeNi alloy. The base alloys Al0.7CoCrFeNi and Al0.7CoCrFeNiV0.5 were obtained by induction melting. The results showed that the presence of vanadium changes the microstructure of the material. In the case of the base alloy, the structure is biphasic with a visible segregation of alloying elements between phases. In contrast, the Al0.7CoCrFeNiV0.5 alloy has a homogeneous solid solution bcc structure. The presence of vanadium increased hardness by 33%, while it significantly reduced friction wear by 73%.
